Synopsis:
After the party has slain a group of undead scholars, the judge of death--Jergal--climbs out of his sarcophagus to greet them. He has been locked inside for years by the god Helm to atone for his part in raising the Dead Three, wicked gods who are now plotting to conquer the realms. Jergal is emotionless and excessively formal, both resigned to his fate and that of others. He is here to assist the party because that is his divine oath, not out of any true desire to act. Players can attempt to goad or attack him, but to minimal effect, as he is functionally immortal. His only goal was to see their faces, so he can find them at camp later to offer further assistance.

Jergal (appearing as Withers) climbs out to inspect the living; he is excessively formal, resigned, and bound by a divine oath to assist the party even though he feels no real desire to act. He asks a calm, philosophical question about the worth of a mortal life largely to observe the party and commit their faces to memory, then promises to find them later at camp to offer further help. Though players may try to provoke or attack him, he is functionally immortal and largely unaffected; the dialogue excerpts show a few possible player answers but do not exhaust all choices.

context: The party has just killed a group of undead scholars in a tomb and awakened Jergal, the ancient judge of death, who had been sealed in a sarcophagus by the god Helm as penance for his role in raising the Dead Three. He appears in the guise of Withers, is excessively formal and emotionally resigned, and is compelled by a divine oath to aid the living even though he feels no real desire to help. Jergal's immediate purpose is observational—he asks a quiet, philosophical question to study the party and commit their faces to memory, then promises to find them later at camp to offer further assistance (including resurrection services). Players can try to provoke or attack him, but he is effectively immortal and largely unaffected; his cooperation stems from penance, not goodwill.
